blocks.x: Go on. Manuel Sayers, 29 to first 61. Now then, Manuel, can you tell us when you first started playing?
Well, I actually first started playing was in a professional, I'd say, back in 1920, about April of 1924.
Yeah, but you've been playing as a kid before then?

Well, I'd say, well, when I was going to school and I'd play like weekend jobs, you know. Maybe Friday and Saturday, Friday and Saturday and Sunday. And the band that I was, we were all taking lessons from the same professor, Dave Perkins.
Oh, Dave Perkins, yeah.
Yeah, he lived there on 6th between Rides and Verón.
How old were you when you were going for these lessons?
Oh, I must have been around about, let's see, two, I must have been around about 15, 16 years old.
Oh, yeah. Did anybody in your family play instruments? I mean, where did you get the idea you wanted to play an instrument?
Well, my father was a musician. He played guitar and played viola, played a little bass. What was his name? George Sayle.
Yeah.

And he played with the band they called that, they called the band the Silver Leaf Band. Oh, Silver Leaf Band. Yeah, that was Alvin Nicholas. I remember he was the lead. He played violin and sax. But the band was the Silver Leaf Band. And the trio consisted of guitar, violin and bass. And I just remember who the bass player was.
And you picked it up more or less from your father then?

Well, yes. When my father, I remember he'd taken the three brothers up. My oldest brother and my brother Joy and myself. And he used to always see me fool around with the guitar. And so he got the three of us together and he showed us a little chord and everything. And it seemed like I was the one that kind of grasped the idea kind of quickly about the grappling of the chord. So, yeah, I remember the first number he showed me how to play was Go Feather Your Nest.
Oh, yeah.

Because Bradford's funny story is still using the theme song. Mm-hmm. And after the Irish got so good with that, he decided, well, I should study something real, what he thought would really pay off the violin.
Yeah.
So this friend, him and Mr. Dave Perkins, they were good friends. My dad had come from out the Irish Channel.
Yeah.

And so he talked to Mr. Dave and so he told me that Mr. Perkins didn't want to teach no violin. He wasn't bothered by teaching, you know, because he was actually a brass band teacher. Yeah. So he kind of talked a minute and he said, well, okay, I'll send him over. And I was going to school and I had a little job. Like most boys had a job going to school and like yard boy, you know, cleaning up. And I didn't pay but 75 cents a week.
Oh.
So, yeah, and the lesson, Dave Perkins was charging me 75 cents. Yeah. That just took all my little change there, you know. Yeah. I think I started violin in about, I believe, about two years or so.
That's with Dave Perkins.
Yeah, with Dave Perkins.
He was a good teacher.

Oh, yeah. She was, I mean, he didn't actually play the violin, but he understand the fundamental of it. And he, like in teaching all the instruments, he knew music well, you know. In fact, and I used to have a little job, I used to pick up a little change from him. Like around this time here, he would be getting those instruments fixed up because he rented instruments with the guys, you see.
That would be about countable time.

Yeah, right around now. And he would clean them up and maybe sign them up. And he'd do a few little repairs like putting corks in the valves and things. I mean, the water valves, you know. And I picked up those change like that. Did he have many pupils? Who? Dave Perkins had a lot of pupils. Oh, yes, yes. He taught white and colored, yeah. Yes.
He was a very light fellow, wasn't he?
Very light. He played in brass band. He played sousie bone. Sometimes he played trombone and maybe baritone. Yeah.
I believe Baby Dodd studied under him for a time.

Well, that was one time. I probably, I know a lot of musicians were responsible and got their training for them. Yeah. Maybe they didn't stay long, but if they didn't get their training, they'd come down there and borrow instruments, you know. Yeah.
Where did you go to after Dave Perkins? Did you go to any other teachers?

Well, no. Like I said, this little, this band, they were all fellows older than me because I was just about 18, if I remember well. And they were all the trombone players named George Morris and the trombone players named Thomas Mack. And the clarinet player was named Edmund Washington.
Oh, yeah.

And we used to rehearse around there and we used to go to the trombone house and rehearse. I was on 8 and Liberty and I had a cousin, Ray Fielder. And he was playing drum, but every Sunday, remember, we used to rehearse on them. And some fella came in town by the name of Joe Wynn, looking for a band, and they got in the word of it. And so they made a deal with him. And the only thing about the deal was this fella, Joe Wynn, played drum.
Uh-huh.

And there was a job in Pensacola and I was still going to school. So in order to take the job, we had to leave my cousin behind, you see. Oh, yeah. And he didn't like that so well, so we had promised him when we'd get over there and we'd get around and everything and everything. Well, we would get rid of this guy and then send for him, you see. For sure, we, my mother didn't want me to go. My father said, well, you better let him go because it looks like that's what he wants to be, a musician. So I was in ninth grade, I remember, 30, McDonald's 35 High School. That's around about April of 1924.
Oh, yeah.

So we left. We went to Pensacola, Florida. And when we got there, we took up a piano player. I can't think of the woman's name right now. And we played for a doctor named. There was two fellas running a baseball park there. There was one, Dr. Burgundy, and the guy that was under Meatmark was named Mary and Long. It was sort of a corporation. They ran this baseball park with named Moore Castle Park. And they had a colored ball team. We used to play like Mobile and Montgomery all around that vicinity.
But did you always play guitar in the early days or did you play banjo as well?

No, well, you see, after I'd been playing with this band, I was, my oldest brother was working for a world artist. And he bought a banjo and I was teaching him how to play the banjo. And at the same time, I was learning myself.
Oh, yeah.
So he got this instinct with it, so I started fooling around. That's why I started playing banjo in this particular band, because we were all still scholars of the important.
But you never took lessons on the banjo?

I practically taught myself that at that time, you see. Yeah, because I could read, I mean, from playing the violin. I used to use the violin school to get the idea with it and then look at the chords on the piano part and write them down, you know, and play them on the banjo.
So you only took lessons from Perkins on violin.
Violin, that's right. Not on guitar.
How did you come by picking up a guitar?

Well, as I said at first, that was the first thing my dad had tested me out on. He tested me out on that guitar, and he saw why I thought I should pick up some, well, like a lead instrument, you know.
So you could play a bit of a guitar when you went to Perkins?

Oh, yeah, yeah. Well, by me, from my head, from where my dad taught me, no music, and I just taught me a few chords, you know. And what was the first band you played with? Well, this particular band, that was named, we called the band All-Star.
Oh, yeah.

We were playing around there, around like a million boys, and we'd play, I remember what they, that day they'd call it, Pilot Land, but that's all out there. And, well, I ended up on the other side of Gentile, Jefferson, I mean, St. Fennard Avenue, that's all built up now. You see, I was doing progression there, I remember that as well.
Who did you say was in that band?
Oh, the leader was named George Morris, a trombone player, and a trumpet player was named Thomas Mack. And Edmund Washington. We all had, we were taking lessons from this, Sam, for the Perkins. Yeah.
Oh, you were all taking lessons together?
Yeah. Oh. And we just, we called ourselves, we were practicing and trying to, you know, get ourselves familiar with playing together, see.
What kind of songs would you play?

Oh, those times when we played, well, I understand the tune of those times, like, you had to play Tiger, Egg, you had to play, I remember Bucket's got a hole in it. And, oh, they had a lack of blues, you may play in B-flat or F or something like that, you know.
How would they, how would the banjo play on that? Was it straight 4-4 or what'd you do like?

Well, it was, well, I can learn it then, I mean, I first started out playing straight 4-4, and after a while I used to listen to that banjo player like John Morrell, he was very popular and good. And the other ones, that boy named Pley, a little blackie, Santiago. Santiago. His uncle played a very nice banjo. I remember he was playing at a place called Eli Beans that was running that place then. When I was young, I used to stand on the outside and listen at him, you see. That's how I developed ideas about playing, you know, about, if none of them were trying to get an idea how the banjo should be played, see. Yeah. Yeah.
And, uh, that was, uh, most of the numbers you would play, like Tiger, Egg, and Bucket, uh.

Yeah, I see, those were the popular numbers. Yeah, the standard numbers. And then you had a little popular tune, because we all could read, and we'd buy the little stocks that thing was out, you know, you know.
That was an old reading band, you could all read?

Well, we could all read, yeah. Drummer, too? Yeah, even Joe Wynn could read. My curtain could read, yeah. But we did, like I said, we did a lot of faking and everything, yeah. And sometimes it, it, uh, you'd go and maybe get the lead part, and then you'd have to fake your cards, you know, or something like that. And then we'd go down and buy stock, you see.
Can you remember who was, uh, the most popular band in New Orleans around that time?
Oh, yeah. Who did you go and listen to?
Well, yeah.

Well, Kid Randy was playing at the Bullets Club. I was living on a rampart between, uh, six and Washington, and the Bullets Club was up there on the eight, and, and what they call it, Dan Neal now. Mm-hmm. And that was, that was, that was much, that was every Monday night, they had a big dance there. Then they had the Santa Singers, or the San Suu Club, or they used to call it Howard Street, but they called it La Salle now.
Mm-hmm.
And then, uh, they had, uh, another place up on Amelia Street, uh, the only nickname they gave, they used to call it the Bucket of Blood.
Oh, yeah.
And there was another place there on, on Franklin, between Jackson and, and Phillip.
And Rene would play at all those places?
No, not Rene, I mean, that was a different band. Oh, yeah. Rene played at the Bullets at that time, most of the time.
Mm-hmm. Who did Rene have on banjo? Can you remember?
Yes, there was, uh, one fella named Son, and then he had a fella, we used to call him, he was really from the island, we called him a Jewmaker.
Mm-hmm.
I can't think of his name now, but, uh, he, he played a very nice banjo.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
And did the rest of the band go with you and listen to Rene and those?

Oh, yeah, we all did that, all. You tried to play like them? Yeah, we all, like I said, you had to try to find some kind of way to hide the instrument, which would be played. And there was another band you played with Rene, I think we called him Son, Son of Sonny. Yeah, he was a little short spell, he all looked like he was sleeping all the time, yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. I didn't know. We had the Rene band that time, I remember at the Bulls, there was Rene on trumpet, and Zeb on clarinet, and, uh, Chani, what they call, which his name is, Abbie Forrester, on drums.
Oh, yeah, Chani.
And, uh, Simon Murray on bass.
Yeah.
And, uh, and, uh, sometime Rene would use his, uh, his brother on drums.
Joe Rene.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah.
And, uh, where did you go after this band, you know what I mean?

Well, after, like I said, we went out to Florida, in Pensacola, Florida, we stayed out there about a year and nine months. Mm-hmm. And, uh, the band, we got out there, the people gave us a name, they started calling us the Pensacola Jazzers.
Yeah, yeah.
You see, but, uh, there was another player, a fellow had an undertaker named Prince Morris.
Mm-hmm.
And he had hired a band, they was already out there, that was Lee Collins.
Oh, yeah.
It was a Lee Collins group, and he had, uh, Lee Collins on trumpet, he had, uh, uh, uh, what was his brother? You see, it was Percy Willie and...
What?
Oh, yeah, well, yeah. Oil on trombone.
Yeah.
And, uh, Evan Hall on clarinet. Mm-hmm. Al Morgan on bass. Mm-hmm. And I believe he had Joe Strada on drums, yeah. And had a very fine banjo player in those days named Caffrey.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Yeah. So, uh...
And they were playing at the same time as you and Pennsylvania.
Yeah, they were playing with a fellow named Prince Morris.
Mm-hmm.

So, uh, they had some trouble about their money with Prince Morris, and this fellow, Joe Wynn, he, uh, he took Al Morgan and, and, uh, Edmund Hall out of that band. Oh, yeah. See, and put them with us. Yeah. Then we had another, we got another woman piano player named Helen Jackson.
Yeah.
She was originally from there. But his first piano player was named Beck. Come back to me now. She was named Beck.
Oh, yeah.
And the one that, uh, when they made the change, in other words, the lawyers in the band, that's why we picked up Al Morgan, Edmund Hall, and picked up a piano player named Helen Jackson.
Mm-hmm.
That was the band that consisted, so, uh...
That was your seven-piece band?
Yeah. So, uh, we took, uh, Hall at, uh, bought him a sax. He wasn't playing sax then.
Edmund Hall?
Yeah.
Yeah.

And bought him, I think he bought him a C-melody brass sax, I remember well. And, um, well, he couldn't read so much, but Edmund Washington could read, so what we'd do, we'd buy numbers, like, stock numbers, and run them down. Well, Edmund Hall had such a good year, you know. He'd play, uh, he'd learn to lead, and then Edmund Washington would play and play, and maybe the other part, maybe the third hour to the part, see, something like that, see. And then he would double on, climb out on certain numbers, you see, because we had one number that was real famous, uh, uh, for us, uh, let's see, what the name of that thing, uh, uh, uh, uh, it'll never come to me later. But anyhow, the number that we played was just like, I said we played then, like we had, that was a tiger leg, you had, uh, Buckley got a hole in it. And then I remember, uh, a number of pop tunes came out there, uh, I can't see, but anyhow, that was in, like I said, 24. All the numbers that came out, like, in stock, we'd buy them, because that was the trend then, you know, and then we'd keep up like, you know, all these blues and things like that, the people liked that, you know. And, uh...
And when did you go after this band broke up?

Well, as I said, we, we, in Pensacola, we were working for these people, and so, uh, we used to play a town like, like Mobile, and go to Montgomery, and, uh, there's a couple other times we'd go. So, uh, around about, uh, let's see, close to 26, well, we left Pensacola, no, we made a trip down to Florida, that's what we made, a trip all over from Pensacola to, uh, Jacksonville, Florida. Well, this guy, here in the...

he was managing the band and booking the band because they didn't have no bookies no day, but he was a man that knew a lot of people, you see. And we booked this all the way to Jacksonville. We stayed, I remember it was in the winter we were in Jacksonville, Florida. And the fella George Morris, he had been a cook one time. He suggested that we go down to Miami or Panama, way down up in there, you see. And well, the fella, they wasn't doing so good on the road and everybody wanted to get back to Pensacola, you see. But that was one of the mistakes we made because the kind of band we had, people out there, all the way we played, they took to the band because they could dance by these, and they had different New Orleans temper to it, and they had never heard anything like that, because in automobile they had a, people used to dance by a brass band. The brass band was, I think it was named after Pope, no, it was named after the Tuxedo Band, like Tuxedo here. Yeah, had a brass band, and then in Jacksonville, they had a band around there named Eagle Eye. That was a dance band, and they had another band, a brass band, like I say, all the places there, the people had brass band, they were dancing by them, but they didn't have that New Orleans swing to it, you know. But we made a mistake by not going down further in south in Florida. So we came back to Pensacola, and like I said, the thing was good, so we went over, all of us went over to Mobile. Well, they had a union in Mobile, well they kept us from working in a lot of places, but we used to work a hotel called, I think it was the Battle House Hotel in Mobile. Those people used to request us because they'd hire bands like Sam Morgan and Buddy Petit from New Orleans, you know, but we were already down there, so they would hire us, you know. So, I think it was around about 26 or something, I, uh, see, see, no, first, Edmund Hall had got a letter from a fellow named Eagle Eye in Florida, in Jacksonville, Florida, and he wanted Edmund, Al Morgan, and me. So I had to, so Al had, Al Morgan had already left and come back to New Orleans, and I decided, I said, well, I don't want to stay around, either I, I left the band in Mobile. So, uh, Edmund Hall took, uh, took him, uh, took Cootie and a fellow named Frank Jackson on band, Cootie the trumpet player. Cootie, what was that? Yeah, Cootie William, yeah. Cootie William? Cootie William, yeah, he's really from around, he was around that end. He was, he had one guy that could pick up on how the New Orleans guys were playing, they went and joined this guy, Eagle Eye, so in the later years, I found out that they made a tour and went to New York, and that's where, uh, Cootie and, uh, and Edmund Hall left the band and stayed in New York. Yeah. See, and that's how they actually went to New York, yeah. How did you come to, uh, get in with Lee Collins and David Jones with the Astoria? Well, that, that was way back from there, and coming back, so when I came back here in, like I said, 26, well, uh, my daddy knew me very, very well, you see, and they had, uh, Celestine and B.B. Ridley had split up, you see. Yeah. And, um, Celestine had his own band. When was it split up? That's around about 26, yeah. 26. Yeah, but I can ride in steelware, but, uh, I'd say about a year and, uh, I mean a year and nine months, so I'd say about 26. Well, anyhow, when I came back here, um, uh, uh, uh, originally, that's, uh, B.B. William's brother was running the Pelican for fallback, and they had, hadn't so long built this place up, and there was a nice ballroom and everything, they was having them dancing, I think, three times a week. So, uh, that was B.B. Ridley band, and he had, uh, B.B. Ridley on trumpet, uh, on the trombone, he had shots on trumpet, and he had another, yeah, shots of Madison, and he had another trumpet player named Bat Brown, and he on trombone, and, uh, the, the read section was first, uh, a fellow named Joe, I believe Joe Watson, I believe he's a clandest saxophone player, and they had, uh, Robert Hall. That's Ed's brother? Yeah, uh, uh, uh, that's his brother, yeah, the Evan brother, and they had another fellow, I can't even think of his name, so, uh, in the rhythm section, they see, they had Happy on drum. Happy Goalson? Yeah, Happy on Goalson, and the M.B. on piano, and, uh, they had another bass player when I came, and I think that's when they took, uh, John Porter on bass, because he hadn't so long come, he come in town, they tell me from, uh, on the road with a show. So, a little later, David Jones came in town, and he hired David Jones, and that was a very good band, that was about, uh, about a 10-piece band, I believe. What was the name of that band? Well, they, they call it the Pelican Band, that's what they call it after. It was really, yeah, he was the leader. So, we worked there, I think about, I don't know, about quite a year, and, uh, some kind of, uh, uh, the big original, and his brother, Manuel, had fallen out. And we had a job, uh, a fellow named, um, Jack Sheen, had opened up the suburban, had built the suburban garden, and we, uh, here, here, at Hyatt Village, the band opened up the place, see, and so we opened up that place, and we stayed there, we made nice money there, and, uh, they were raiding the place like they were doing, you know, and everything, so, Jack decided to close up a while, see. Well, when we left there, we got a job at, um, where Pete Herman is now, they used to call it the Club Plantation, and that's where, uh, they just made the band smaller, you know. That's where Cotshell got with us, too. And, uh, well, them were still on piano, shots on trumpet, and David Jones, and one time Handy played there with us, too. John Handy? Yeah, John Handy played with us, that was still the favorite of the band. He was playing clarinet then, was he? Yeah, he was just coming on sax, you see, because Clannery was kind of little guys, well, playing Clannery, they were, you know, going on sax. Yeah. Sax was being popular. So, when that, uh, job closed up, I think that's when I went on the, on the boat with Faith Marvel. Yeah. What, what boat would that be? That was the, uh, Steaming Capital. Capital. Mm-hmm. That was around, I'd say, about, uh, 27 and part of 28. Do you remember who was in that band at that time? The Faith Marvel? Yeah. Oh, yeah, uh, the, the trumpet, the brass section was, uh, Albert Snye, and they had a little trumpet player from St. Louis called Eckhart. Mm-hmm. They had a trombone player. We used to call him Geechee. He wasn't familiar. He was from, actually, from South Carolina. Not Geechee Fields. I don't know. He was short, dog-browns, fella. Yeah. Played a lot of trombone. He had been playing around with circus and sides, too. Oh, yeah. You know, he's a very funny and comedian, fella. Mm-hmm. And, uh, in the rhythm section was Faith Marvel, piano, and that fellow named, drummer named Gene Hill, Al Morgan on bass, and me on banjo. Mm-hmm. Because I had took, I had taken, you know, Willie Foster's place when they let him go. Oh, yeah. And, uh, the saxophone section was, uh, uh, let's see, Willie, uh, Willie Humphrey was in there playing, I think, third sax. Yeah. And Clannett, and the Horace Ubank, I think, was playing in first sax, and, uh, uh, Rollins was on tenor. Oh, yeah. Yeah. That was, that was, uh, that was, uh, the sax section. So, how long did you stay with them? Well, I stayed with them. I remember I played the winter with them, and I went to the winter, summer for them to go to St. Louis. I stayed a whole summer in there, and on the way, coming back in September, they used to come back this way. I was, they let me go in, in September in Memphis. I never forget, they took, uh, banjo and play with them. They had played there before, and they used to call him Red. That's all I know. Yeah. Yeah. So, when I, when I, uh, came back from then, well, I went back with the Bay Rizzley band, and I stayed. That still had the same personnel, did it? Yeah, well, we were doing, they were doing, like, you know, like job and gig in the call. He wasn't working anywhere, I still, yeah. Yeah. And, um, I seen I left them, I think, I'm not going to go a year. I went to the, uh, I believe it was Sidney Desbyne, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, I went with Sidney Desbyne and played with his band about a, oh, I guess about a year, a little over a year or something. Do you remember who was in that band? Sidney Desbyne? Oh, yeah. Uh, Sidney Trumpet, leader, and the next trumpet was Gene Hall. Nelson was on trombone. Which Nautson was that? Sam Nelson, I don't know. Lewis Nautson? Lewis Nelson, trombone. And, uh, the sax section was, the sax section was, uh, was Thetto, Altu, Thetto Poinnell, David John on tenor, and, uh, Alexander, Tats. Tats was playing first. Adolf Alexander. Adolf Alexander. Yeah. And the rhythm section was, uh, let's see, we had, we were using, um, our shoulder blanching, and, um, let's see what we had on there, Ransom Island on bass, and, uh, a little fella named Bucket. He came here from Chicago. He stayed around here quite a while, and me on, I think I was playing banjo and, and straight guitar then. Yeah. That was in 1930, I remember where it was, because we left, and went all the way up to St. Paul, and that was the first year they had, because they had built that Haston lock on the other side of Red Wing.
You missed out the, uh, the Lee Collins period there. Well, I, well, that, oh, yeah, that's right,

that's right. That was, that was before Sidney Desmond, I mean Sidney Desmond, because there was, there was a fella named John Morell, banjo player. He had a job at the La Vida, as a jitney dance. That's right. And, um, and that band was, the leader was John Morell, the banjo player, and, uh, Lee Collins on trumpet. Thereto Poinnell on alto and David Jones on tenor. Yeah. Uh, Joe Rovershaw on piano, uh, and, uh, Albert Martin, I think, the drummer. Oh, Albert Martin. Yeah. On drum, and I took John Morell's play. Well, we played, we wait there, and, uh, and then Lee Collins got, uh, and through Lee Collins and David Jones, the, uh, uh, Binge was open up, uh, on the top of the Astoria. Yeah. They used to call it Astoria Garden or something like that, club. Well, it was a nightclub. Well, at that time, the Lyric Theater was, it was, uh, was closed in that year, and they had a show here, and they were just training around here, so Binge got the idea of taking the show and, and building this band with, uh, with Lee Collins and David Jones as the leader of it, see. This, this Binge fellow, he's the guy? Sam Binge, that, you know, that, where we played at Fowler, that place, on Royal Street, yeah, yeah. So, um, we worked there. I think that's why we made that, uh, that record while we were making, working there, because we used to play those numbers every night, I remember. Tell me about that, uh, recording date. How did you come by that? Well, that was, Lee Collins, that was true, Lee Collins. This fellow, uh, was named the same fellow on the Southland, I believe? Was that, that was the same, Mares? Yeah, Mares. Yeah, well, he liked it, Lee and everything, and some fellas had told him that they, they should record Lee, so, I think the company came from, from New York. It was Victor Company. Yeah, Victor, that's right, it was, on, on the Bluebird, Bluebird record, yeah. Well, we, we, we, we made that recording down at, uh, the Italian Hall on Espanola. Yeah. Uh-huh. What time of day was that when you started? Can you remember? Oh, we started that when we got there in the morning around about nine or ten o'clock, I'll never forget. Yeah, I think we stayed there until about six or seven o'clock that evening. Yeah? Mm-hmm. It was a pretty, uh, wet day, wasn't it? Yeah, it was raining, and, uh, and, uh, I wouldn't say it was so cold, but, I mean, the window was long, New Orleans rain, you see? Is that where you got the name of that tune from? Yeah, Damp Weather. Well, our first tune we had, I remember we got together was Astor, Strut, and, uh, uh, now, maybe you can tell me, uh, those are the tunes we were hoisting on. Tip Easy Blues. No, that, we made that up in the station, at the, at the, well, at the, during the recording, and also Damp Weather. And, uh, Duet Stump? Yeah, Duet Stump. Those two were the real numbers that we had really gotten down really good together, see? Yeah. So, the other time, we just made them up, like you said, the one blues, and one guy said, well, go ahead, rain, I'll just name it,
this damp weather, see? Everybody was kind of white. And there wasn't one named Tip Easy or something? Tip Easy. Yeah, like, well, we had all,

I was doing probation day, and we had some, uh, stuff from Benny Hall. We used to buy all our stuff from that, so we called that the Tip Seas, yeah. Yeah. And in that session, now, Albert, um, Martin had gone with, um, a fellow named Don Albert. Yeah. Because he came through town to Texas, and he had, um, he took members, they took fellows out of three or four bands around here, you see? And I was supposed to go over them, too, but I had already had this offer to go with sitting Desvino on the boat, you see? And, uh, that's where I, I didn't go, so, uh, that's why they picked up Joe Strada. Joe Strada. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Picked him up, that's why he was actually on the session. Yeah. So it wasn't Albert Martin on the session? No,

no, no. He, he, he was already out of town in Texas. Yeah. So, um, when they tell him it come time for the boat to leave, well, I had told him to put my notice in it, and I had recommended, which they all liked it, Danny Barker. Yeah. That's how Danny Barker got in there. That was right after the recording, was it? Yeah, shortly after the recording, yeah. Mm-hmm. And, um, I don't know, on the record, they used Rennie Hall, but I don't know, Rennie might have played, like, when I have, when I was out of town after Danny Barker left, because, uh, how that happened with Danny Barker, they had a trip to go on. You know, all these, those days, used to have excursions running from Chicago to New York, New Orleans to Chicago, and they used to hire a band. Well, Lee Collin had that job, too, you see, and I didn't want that,
because I was satisfied going on the boat. But it was you on all, all, all the records then? Oh, yeah,

I was definitely there. Yeah. I was definitely there. I did a, I don't know, somewhere that he messed that up. Well, anyhow, when they went to Chicago on this excursion, Danny went up, went with him. Danny was with the band, and that's where, uh, they met Louis Armstrong, and they did a little, like we do, around your
ballyhoo, and you know what I mean, on a truck, you know. Yeah, I know what you mean. And they told me

they met Louis and everything, and that's where Danny met his uncle Paul, you see. And Paul got him died, Danny died, and he should come to Chicago, and he could work, and I think that's how Danny went to Chicago, and he went to New York. Who was that Paul? Danny, Paul Barber. Oh, Paul Barber. Yeah, he was with Louis Armstrong at that time in Chicago. Yeah. Mm-hmm. So the only thing I say, I was working on a book when I heard about that, so, um, that was, that was in 1930, I remember very well. Where did you go after the boat? Well, when we came on, the season was over, well, I stayed with Sidney, I think I stayed with Sidney band about a year and a half, almost two years, yeah, because we were pretty good together. Then, uh, he let me go around about, I say about 1933, because at that time, Peter Horn had broke up his old band, and he was, there was a band around there that called, uh, Southern Syncopators or something like that.
Mm-hmm. Now, uh, who was in this Southern Syncopators? Can you remember, man?

Yeah, in the Southern, uh, Syncopators, there was, uh, Eddie Pearson on trombone, Leo Dejo trumpet, and a trumpet player named DeRuxa, DeRuxa, DeRuxa from over the river. Mm-hmm. And the sax section was, uh, Elliot Taylor. Mm-hmm. Uh, Arthur Durbney, Joe Ruzon. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. And, uh, rhythm section was Sidney Montague, I believe Booker Washington on bass, and Allegretto on piano.
Mm-hmm.

I don't remember them using any bands, you know, it might have been Sidney Fluge, or, no, I don't remember the bands that played that. Well, that's the band that, um, when Peter had the idea of this band, this original band, they used to play, he used to take dates, and, uh, he'd hire this band because at that time there was...

that old band, Pulon band was about, I believe about six pieces or so, and ten, eight and ten piece band were coming, becoming popular then. And then there was the younger musicians, you know, so I remember I was working with Sidney Desby and he had let me go for Randy Hall.
Oh yeah.

I was staying on La Hop, La Hop and La Prusse, I believe it was, and Randy was staying right across the street from me. So, well like I said, at that time in working with the big band, I'd always work with some guys with maybe two or three pieces like Ryan Young and Frank's Quarter when the big band wasn't doing nothing. And I was doing a little range in that time for the band. Yeah. So when the word got around and Sidney had let me go, well, I remember Leo Dazio came to my house because he had one of the guys that had recommended me highly, see, in the band. So he asked me would I join them because he had heard that I wasn't with Sidney. I said, well, yes, you know. And they were working out at the Orange Country Club. They had three nights out there a week. I remember it was Friday, Saturday, and Sunday evening. Well, that was pretty good money, you know, as of now to a day. So I went to rehearsal. They were rehearsing on Ivor Street at the Piano Playhouse. His name was Alla Greta.
Oh, yeah.

Yeah, he was arranging for the band. And in the band I remember well, there was Peter On the Leader, a violin player. The sax section was Arthur Durbin, Elliot Taylor, and Joe Ruzon. Elliot Taylor played Clannett in sax at that time. It was very good. I think Arthur Durbin was the first sax and he did a little singing. And in the rhythm section were Alla Greta on piano. He was very young. He was one of the young fellas. And Alfred William was on drums, Simon Moreau on bass, and me on banjo. I was playing banjo and guitar. Oh, yeah. So I remember well in playing at the New Orleans Country Club, Mr. Crawford Ellis, I believe he was president of something like that. He was the one that got Peter on the band. And I remember one thing was on a Saturday night. Captain Boyne and his wife were out there. Well, I knew the captain, you know. And he came over and spoke to the band. He recognized me. And that's how we got the job on the boat.
What year was that about?

Oh, that was in, let's see, about around 33. 33, yeah. So I remember Captain Boyne came over and talked to Peter on and told him he wanted to come down to the office and see him. You know, he said he'd like to have his band and he'd like to have him on the boat. And he spoke to me and he said, yeah, I said, that's sales. He said, sales have worked for us, which I had already worked with Pete Marvillin and sitting in there's being banned on the boat. So Peter on asked me about it. I told him, I said, well, that's a good job. I said, he said, well, I do. Tip Captain Boyan Strecker had requested that Peter Bogart would take charge of the band, because like I said, the young fellas in there, like I was up in the East, and Booker was living there, but I mean, they just thought they would look too young to have, because Eddie Pearson wanted to take charge, but they wouldn't let him take charge, see. So Peter Bogart was lead, I think Eddie Pearson was sort of a manager, like, see. So I really missed Peter on that particular year, and we, that particular year we closed, we usually come back here, but we closed in St. Louis, and I remember it was the last week in August, if I remember right, and I stayed around St. Louis about a week or so, and I had a person, a very good friend of mine, had lived in Chicago, and he used to always ask me to come up there, you see, so I thought that was a fine time for me to go up there and see him, and then...
Who was this fellow?

His name was Joe Bradford, a friend of mine, so I wrote a term, he told me, yes, come on up, see, so he was married and he had two daughters, and one of the girls was born while I was staying with him, so he made it so pleasant and so nice for me, like, saying I didn't have to pay a whole lot of money, and then he gave me a time to get around and make connection, you see, so well, it took me about nine months before I could actually find Wake, you know, So I finally found Wake, well, I stayed with him until about, uh, oh, I think about 40 or 41 or 43, anyhow, it was during the war, I remember, and, uh, I got married up there, and, uh, like I said, that was the time I had put down, uh, playing with the band because there wasn't so much work, I started playing with a small combination, like three, four pieces, you know. What year was that? That was around, uh, well, I say I, I, uh, I would have left the boat in 38, and I got in Chicago around September 1938, yeah, and I actually didn't start working until around, around about, uh, around about 39, see, and, uh, I had, uh, there was a couple of, uh, two places, one fellow was, uh, at Booker in Asia, one was on State Street, and one was on, uh, South Park, so you could go around there, and the guys, if they had something on the weekend, well, they, you know, they'd hire, you see. And about me playing electric and having electric guitar, well, I got quite a few jobs like that because there wasn't too many fellows with electric guitars around, around Chicago.
Who else worked for you in this trio you had there?

Well, this trio started, we started from a band with, uh, Oliver Beathen, I forget, he had a, some book ahead of gave him a contract to go on the road, and we used to hush around at, uh, the local in Chicago, and it was about, uh, 10 or 15 piece band, but when they, and, uh, the bass player and the violin player, they were in the band, so we had got a couple little jobs, just the three of us, and that's where we decided that we should organize the trio. So when the band got ready to go away, well, we didn't go away when I'm on the road, see, so we called, we got a job to the local, I remember, on the west side of Chicago, and, uh, people seemed to like what we were doing because we were playing and doing a little singing and harmonizing and everything. So we got another job at a place called the Bar of Music on Howard Street, and, uh...
What was the band calling them?
Well, this was the trio.
Yeah, did it have a name, the trio?

Yeah, I said, I'm thinking, say, how we got the name, so when we got that, it wouldn't want to ask us for a name, so we started calling us Jump This and something like that, and, uh, so, uh, the place was named the Bar of Music. They always started calling it Chocolate, something like that, so the woman said, she didn't like that, she said, well, I'm going to put two names together, I'm going to use the Chocolate Bar of Music. So, uh, that's how we got, uh, then we stayed there and made a pretty good, you know, hit there and everything, and then we got with a booker, and we start, uh, going out of town. I remember we got with a hotel chain, and we played, uh, what's the time with Stu Baker, uh, South Bend, Indiana. We played, uh, uh, Dayton, Ohio, uh, Canton, Ohio, and, uh, and played Cleveland. Well, this, uh, uh, trio, and we played quite a few places around Chicago, uh, and, uh, we broke up, I guess, about, uh, 46 or so, and I, uh, didn't do nothing for a while, then I got hired about to organize my own group, and I had a group, uh, I used a fellow named Sam Kazma on guitar and myself on guitar. Uh, had a piano player named Art Terry, and the bass player was Johnny Lindsay. Oh, yeah. He used to be an extramo player from there. Uh, so that stayed up for a while, and, well, I guess about a year or so, and, uh, that broke up, and, uh, I got with a saxophone player. It was, uh, odd combination, a good saxophone player, I can't think of his name right now, but it was a bass player, sax, it was me on electric guitar. Mm-hmm.
What year would that be?

Oh, that was around about, uh, about 47, I say, part of 48, because, uh, when that job closed down, well, I stopped playing for a while, and I, I got my job working in a plane, because I was married then, see, and I stayed out there for about four or five months, work got slowed and laid me off, and, uh, and then, uh, that was 48, yeah, part of 49. So around about, uh, August of 49, I, I made a trip down to New Orleans, to see my mother and father and the family, and, uh, that's what I got, when I came back here, I saw most of the fellas working around my age and everything, where I had most musicians around Chicago had stopped working, they had to go get their jobs, so I decided myself I'd go back and move my stuff and come back to New Orleans. So I got back here, I remember it was after Labor Day. Yeah. Yeah. And I came back here, I, well, I started meeting around my old friends, like, uh, Jimmy Davis and, uh, and, uh, William, and, uh, a couple of other fellas, but I worked with Jimmy Davis, he had a job for me at, uh, show bar, remember, we used to go to work early in the morning, about three or four o'clock, and work.
Jimmy Davis, that's not the bass player?

No, that's the piano player. Oh, yeah. Yeah, Jimmy Davis. And after, uh, I left him, I went with, uh, with O.A. William, and after O.A. William, I, you see, I went with, uh, a nightclub, uh, what's the name of that club, his name at, uh, oh, it's uptown, anyhow, I wouldn't understand, I started playing with different fellas around, and, um, around about 56th or September, I went at the paddock with Russell, with a trio, we played.
Snooker Muscle?

Yeah. We played, uh, well, he was already working as the piano, so they decided to have put two more pieces, a bass player named, uh, Stuart Davis, myself on guitar, and we stayed there, I'd say about three years.
What kind of stuff were you playing then?

Well, we were playing, like, uh, mostly like, uh, trio stuff, we had some instrumental, we did a lot of, singing, we had three-part harmony singing, and Russell would sing, and I would sing, and Stuart would sing, and, uh, and we had some, quite some nice instrumental numbers together.
And you were the house band, Dale?

Well, the house band, well, that was Bill Matthews house band. Bill Matthews was there. Yeah, yeah, mm-hmm. And that was wrong, I think, wrong about, uh, uh, it must have been about 58, or something like that, when, when, when they let us go, see. Well, at that time, I started jobbing around with different fellas and everything, in, uh, I see, 58, 59, yeah. In round about 59, I joined Herbert Leary band during the Mardi Gras season. Mm-hmm. Well, I played that season with him. In round about, uh, 60, I went back with this fella, Jimmy Davis. Mm-hmm. We had a trio, uh, Andrew Johnson on drums, Jimmy Davis on piano, and, uh, me on electric guitar, and we was using Blanche Thomas at the time. Oh, the vocalist, yeah. Vocalist, yeah. Uh, well, we worked places like, uh, the Offshore Lounge, and, uh, and, uh, work at the Coat of Two Sisters. Mm-hmm. And, uh, work at another place out on Gentile called Guy's, Guy's Place, I remember. So, uh, and, uh, then my sister passed in July of 60, and I went out to San Francisco, stayed out there about two weeks, and I went to the place where old irons work, the hangover, the place where, uh, kid already works. I believe they call that, uh, river supplement or waterfront or something.
On the levee?
On the levee, yeah. Yeah.
Did you play out there at all?

No, I just, I didn't take no instrument either, because I went out there to bury my sister, but I went around to those places. Mm-hmm. And I passed through Chicago, coming back, around about, uh, oh, yeah, that was around September, yeah. I stayed around there about ten days, and I went to the musician local, saw friends around there, the president, Harry Gray and Samuel Mitchell, uh, recording secretary, I believe. Mm-hmm. And, uh, when I came back here, the group I was working was still working at the Offshore Lounge, so we had about two more weeks there.
Mm-hmm. That was the Jim Davis?

Yeah, Jim Davis, Jimmy Davis, yeah. That closed, and then, uh, William picked me up in September, and I went to, to Florida. Mm-hmm. To September, October, I believe. We had about five weeks out there.
Mm-hmm.
And when I came back, well, that's where I start, uh, working with, uh, not working, but I mean getting jobs with Emma Barrett and Paul Barberin and, uh, Noon and the Bazooka Man.
Oh, Noon Johnson.

Yeah, and I also got a, guys up to date, uh, through Bill Mathes, you see. Mm-hmm. Yeah. So I think that, that carried me up to the day. I'm just what you say called freelancing, you know? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Playing with, uh, different fellas. Yeah.
Uh, go back to the, uh, going back to the early days a bit, uh, what can you remember about John Marrero, you know? What kind of stuff you remember?

Well, John Marrero was a fine banjo player. I remember him when he played with, uh, the Bay Rizley band, which Celestine was the trumpet player. Mm-hmm. Emma Barrett was the piano player. Uh, uh, Simon was the bass player. And, uh, uh, Paul Barberin was the clarinet and saxophone player. And, uh, I mean, yeah, Chani Fawcett, Abbie Fawcett was on drums, yeah. Oh, yeah. I remember he was a very fine banjo player. Mm-hmm.
Did, uh, were they, you know, you heard the records that he made, uh, John Marrero. Are they good examples of his playing, or did he play four or four most of the time?
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. He had a very, in fact, he was one of the best banjo players we had, Ryan. Yeah.
Cause he did a lot of composing, too, didn't he?
Yeah, I heard he wrote a lot of numbers. He wrote some, uh, swing numbers and jazz numbers, and he wrote some nice ballads. Yeah.
He was going, I guess, when you were coming up, was he? Or?

Oh, no, no. He was, he was, uh, when the last time I saw John, he was working at the La Vida Club, I tell you, when I, when John's calling them. Oh, yeah. I was the one who took his place when he went to New York. Yeah?
Mm-hmm.
Oh, he went to New York. Yeah, that's the last time I saw him, and the next thing I heard, he had died. I don't remember what year, as a present, he died.
Uh, how about his brother Lawrence? What do you know?
Well, Lawrence was, was playing around there. stuff
I don't remember what you wear. Lawrence was playing with a band I used to call the Second Tuxedo Band.
Young Tuxedo?
Young Tuxedo, something like that, yeah. I remember the piano player was named Dwight Newman. His son is the terrific trumpet player we have today, Joe Newman, yeah.
And Lawrence would play a straight 4-4 even.
Yeah, he was mostly a straight 4-4 band. But he wasn't, to me, a good solo like John was.
No, no, no. You remember who taught John Marrero, do you know?
No, I don't. I don't remember that. I know the whole family, but I don't remember who taught him.
Remember who taught Lawrence?
Well, maybe...
John?
I think John was playing before Lawrence, I think. Oh, yeah, yeah. Yeah.
How about George Gaino? What do you know about George Gaino in the other day?

Oh, I met George Gaino, I'd say, around about after I came back from Florida. That was around about 26. But it was a club called Entertainers Club. All musicians used to meet around there, and we'd always get around there sometime, and sit in the jam, you know, and everything. That's where I met George Gaino. That's when I had moved, and family had moved downtown. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
On the riverboats there, you know, you still play the same stuff as you're playing today, that, you know, afterbeat stuff, and solo work, did you do solo work?
Banjo? Yeah. Oh, yes, I did. Yeah, I did a lot of solos, you know. At least, well, they didn't allow banjos too much, but you always had to have some of them with the solo on, you know. Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
And you sit there, and, well, they were most reading bands in those days, like on the boat especially, even the bands around, yeah. They had a lot of...
Because you've always been a reader. Huh? You've always been able to read.
Oh, yeah, yeah. I started out reading, yeah. Yeah.

How about the banjos in the old rougher type bands, you know, the dancehall bands like Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly in there? What did the banjo players in there, did they differ from your type of playing?

Well, each guy had his particular style and playing, you know. Some guys I know, probably they couldn't solo, but sometimes leaders, some leaders wouldn't even permit banjo to solos, you know. Like I said, those days I remember the solo number was well, waiting for the sunrise, and Tiger Rag, you know, that was a muscle and a banjo.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah. There was one fellow named Caffrey, like I said, he was about the best picking man around, you know.
What was his name?
For picking him. His name was Caffrey. He played on the roof garden with Manu Perez's band.
Yeah.

Yeah, I'll see if I can remember. I know Perez was the trumpet and leader. Earl Humphrey was the chime one player, and also Willie played in that band. And they had a piano player, and I can't think of her name now. I think Mercy D was in that band, yeah. Miss Mercy D.
Fields?

Yeah, Fields, yeah. That's right. And I can't think of the name of the drum, but it might have been Big Gordon. Alex Big Gordon. Yeah, it might have been him on the drum, but that was a very fine band too at that time, down on the roof garden. And he used to give Caffrey a lot of solos, because he could pick a band and make it sound like a horn blowing.
You've always been taking solos, I guess.

Oh, yeah, yeah. I mean, I was in the Pensacola band back then, 24 and 25, when I came back here with Bay Ridsley. And I worked on a boat with Fate, because that was a must, certain solos like Tiger Ray, Well Waiting For The Sunrise. I mean, you just have to play those solos.
How many measures would they give you for a solo in those days?
Oh, well, like Well Waiting For The Sunrise, I would mostly like two choruses. And Tiger Ray, there might have been one or two choruses.
And the rest of the bands would play the stops behind you like they do today?

Well, sometimes, yeah, they'd play the stop, or either sometimes they'd just play the straight rhythm and use solo, because, like I said, on the boat, a banjo player had to be a solo. Because they had one guy named Red, and they had one guy named Roberson. I met him in Chicago when I was up there, and those guys were terrific banjo players.
Who did you say was about the best banjo player going when you were a young kid?
Well, like I say around there, I always said John.
John Marrero.

John was the best, yeah. And I had another fellow player with Sidney Desby named Percy Sevier. Well, he wasn't playing so much when he came, but after he had been around, he got to be a very good banjo player too. Then we were like, around in the mid-30s, we had Homer Eugene, we had Randy Hall, and had another fellow named Paul, I can't hear his name, Paul Sufferman, and Sidney Fludger, well, he did a lot of singing, and he also played nice banjo too. I could say, Lawrence Moray was around, but John Moray was in New York at that time, in late, well, I'd say about 36, I remember he had gone, because I was in Levita around, oh yeah, John left here around about 28. I believe he died up in New York. Yeah, he died, I heard about him, yeah, the person there. When I came back to Chicago, well, I went back with the Chocolate Bar's trio,
you know, yeah. So you were working with that trio for quite a while, I guess.
Well, yeah, that's the longest group I've worked with the whole I was in Chicago.
How long was that? Do you work with them?
Well, we started up, I'd say around about, oh, around about 40, and we stayed together, I think, about 44, 45, maybe part of 46.
Gee, still with the same three guys?
Yeah, we created quite a reputation around Chicago, at least playing like cocktail lounge and cabaret.
What did you play then, banjo or guitar?
No, I was playing electric guitar.
Oh, all the time.
Yeah, when I went to Chicago, I had put the banjo down there.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So, you didn't get a chance to play the banjo until you got back to New Orleans.

Oh, I'd say I'd just start playing the banjo, let's see, I was at the paddock, that was, what did I say, 45, 55, 56, 57, and that was probably when I went back on the banjo, I mean, and there was just a few numbers I played then because the people were more crazy about, electric guitar and then we were working with a trio, you know. Every once in a while I used to sit in with the band, with Bill Matthews band sometimes, you know, just sitting a few minutes to play with them.
Hey, going back to you really early, did you, anybody else in the family ever play an intro besides your daddy?

Yeah, my oldest brother, like the one I said, I was teaching him bands, he played for a while, he played with a band around the 30s there called the Robert Clark Band. That was a 10-piece band they had in those days. And they played for around the New Orleans Wild and had a lot of, a few out of town dates and everything.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
Did you ever work with Jelly Roll at all when he was?
Oh, no, no. Jelly Roll, I only heard about him but I've never even seen him.
Yeah.
In fact, I never did see her until I, I was, I went out to San Francisco in July to bury my sister. but I'd heard so much about him.
That was the first time you see him.

I've seen him to myself. I'd heard about him around the hill, you know, but I don't remember, I remember seeing Lewis back then in the way it was from 1916 where he'd be playing in parades and things, you know. Mm-hmm. And when he went away on the boat with Faith Marble, St. Louis and things. Mm-hmm. And when he started recording, I remember Lewis's recording he would put out there, I think, in the 20s, I remember, Gipper Mouth and Gut Bucket Blues because we're all the musicians used to follow his records, you know. Oh, yeah, yeah. We'd listen at them and try to play them somewhat like them, yeah.
Well, what kind of numbers did you play with his Pierron bands, you know, what?

Oh, Pierron had like, well, even his small band was, they used to call it, it was like a society band, you know. They played the smooth swing, you know, and played a lot of music and things and other numbers that they composed among themselves.
Old rhythm?
Huh?
Was it old music, old rhythm?

Yeah, mostly, yeah, most of the band then he was reading. And then when he had a big band, a ten-piece band, it was stock numbers and some of the fellas ranged, you know, ranged in the band to see. And of course, when he went on the boat, had to cut out a lot of the range because the captain didn't go for that. He wanted more so of society bands, you see.
So they never played any blues and things like that?
Well, I wouldn't say it too much about the people on the band. Because the people
wouldn't go for that so much.
No, that type of people that they played for.
Do you ever play with Buddy Petillo, Chris Kelly, Rene?
No, I didn't say play in their band, but I remember Buddy around here and when I was in Florida and I first went there, he had been and left and he went to Montgomery.
Oh, yeah.

I remember very well back in 24. He had been out in Pensacola. But like I say, this place, the club, the entertainment club, all the musicians used to hide me around there and you'd meet all those guys. You know, sometimes we'd sit in and jam and play together, you know.
Where was that? The entertainment club?
The entertainment club, yeah.
Whereabouts was that?
That was, I really call that cruise out. That's right behind Krauss Stuhl.
In New Orleans?
Yeah, in New Orleans. The old 25 was right in that channel. It was one block going down Canal Street.
The big 25, is that the place?
Yeah, the original 25 was right on the corner. And the entertainment was right on the, well on the, going across the street corner like, yeah.
Did you ever play with the bunk or so on?

No, no. I never played with the bunk. No. Well, I remember hearing about him those days and everything, but I mean, I was in Chicago when they picked him up and then he took over with George Lewis Band. I was in Chicago.
Hmm.
Yeah.
How about George? You doing any playing with George?
No, not with his band, but I remember George around there, you know.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Uh, did you ever compose any numbers yourself? I mean, are you a composer?
Oh, I composed Chuppet, I mean, I've never gotten with everything.
I mean, you didn't compose anything on a Johnson Collins record, say, any of that?
No, no, no, I didn't compose anything.
I saw one of the titles there, your name under it.
Well, yeah, well, I mean, those were head numbers we made up right away and we, you know, we pitched in and each guy had to say, well, I want this number and so forth like that, yeah.
Going back to that particular recording date, I mean, did you have any arrangement worked out or did you just play?

Well, no, when that recording, like I say, that duet stomp and that stuart stomp, those numbers were well rehearsed, those two numbers. Well rehearsed. And we were playing on the stuart and we mixed those numbers in our program, you know, because we had, you know, finally we were going to record and we got those two together. The other number we just made over at the station, yeah.
What was your story? Was that a place where White and Colored could go or was it?

No, it was a Colored, a nightclub but White used to come in there because Beansley was running the place and he had a lot of White friends and thing and they'd sit them out, you know, certain parts, you know, for themselves. Also the entertainers club. I believe it was, I believe it was Lala the guy that was running the entertainers club.
Pete Lala?

Yeah, I think so, and I think so, if I ain't got it right. But anyhow, those, in those days and even when when Beansley would run the club behind the old Lyric Theater there, what do they call that? The Elites? Elites, yeah, Elites, yeah. Well, I was a young fellow at the other time. I remember White used to go in those places. They'd go as special guests, you know what I mean? They had their own table and they would feel among themselves because in those days the people of White we wanted to always see the other colored bands and see the colored shows, you know. There was something different from that.
How did Sidney Aroding, the White Clarence, how did he come to get on that date of yours?
Well, I don't know exactly but I know he was a close friend of Lee and I think maybe Mayeth had something to do with that. Yeah.
But he fitted in pretty well, don't he?

Oh, he did, yeah, because we didn't have no rehearsal with him. In fact, I didn't know he was there until I got to where we were at the Italian Hall. But I haven't seen him around and known him around, you know, but he fit in right because those two numbers that we rehearsed good, he fit right in there very well.
That's the kind of numbers you play for the people at the Astoria.
Yeah, those same numbers, we were playing those same numbers.
There was a ballroom, was it? They used to dance there?
Well, it was a nightclub. It had a show, a very good show and even had intermission they had a young lady used to go around and sing at table.
Oh, yeah.

And they had a tap dancer, Joe Toy, and Green. And like I say, the Clare State had closed that year and the show people that went to town and Beans had hired them. See, we had a big production show over there. And all that was rehearsed, we had to rehearse for that. And a fellow named Sherman Cooks, he was the master of ceremony.
Did you read music at that place?
Well, we didn't do too much reading there, no. We could all, like I know David Jones, myself, and Thudder Poirnell, but we didn't do all that was head stuff.
Did you play things like blues there?
Yes, played the old version, blues and E flat, B flat, and the calling blues.
Oh, yeah.

And that was like, well, Panama, right, and High Society, that was out, and we did a lot of following numbers that Lewis was putting out that time, I mean, because Lee could play all those kind of numbers. I remember Mahogany Horse Trump was popping at that time. Lee could play that. Dip him off, well, that was kind of old, but I mean, Lee always just specialized in playing everything that, that Lewis Armstrong would put out, even when you're, when you're smiling, I mean, that was out at that time.
And I used to listen to the Lewis records, I guess.
Well,
yeah,
we all did down there, and you all had some great summer players in those days, too. Yeah, another fellow named Guy Kelly,
Oh, yeah.
He was terrific. Another fellow over the river, looked like a Mexican, I can't remember his name, he was very powerful. And in those days, even Howard was powerful, you know.
Kid Howard.

Kid Howard, yeah, he was plenty powerful. Well, Rene was living, because I think after they left the Astuart, the Beansy hired Rene Band. After Lee's band. Yeah, after we left there, he hired Rene Band. I just remember who was in that band, because I was on the boat when I was out of town. I don't remember just exactly who was in it. But I think I'm most sure he had his brother on drum. I don't know whether Zeb was living and that, I don't remember yet.
Who was the best drummer going around in those days? Can you remember that?

Well, I'll tell you, Chani in his days, back then, I can say from 21, 23, 24, Chani was terrific. But Chani had an accident, he was cut up pretty badly, because when I met him in Florida, that's the reason why he was out there. He was running away from this party that cut him up, you know.
What year would that be, Ben?
That was around, that was in, stuff like stuff

24 and 25. Yeah, because he played with, after this fellow Joe Wynn left and my cousin left where he was Chinese. That's where Chinese met Sid and everything, piano player. And he was, all of us was stiff. And I remember the song he used to sing, the Mark Corina and everything. Yeah. He could sing that.
That's the same one as they got today to talk about.

Yeah, that's very popular today. He could really sing that. And I left, let's see, and I came back in 24, I mean in 26 I think he was still out there. But he never did get back to playing like he used to be, you know.
You think you play the same kind of stuff today as you were playing in the old days or have you changed?
Well, as far as the dictionary, I'd say Sam was playing back in those days.
No, I mean you yourself, a banjo, you know?
Oh yeah, yeah. Still the same stuff? Yeah, I played old Sam and old Sam's when I was back in those days.
Coming back again to your lessons with Perkins, what kind of stuff did he go over with you? Did he give you formal lessons?

Well, I was studying the violin. I remember it was the Otto Lang method I used. In fact, most of his instrument that he taught to use Otto Lang's book. Like it was time on, it was one of the violin, it was Otto Lang method, yeah.
And he taught you to read music?
Oh yeah, I got all my music training from him. In fact, anybody went to him and got to be a very good reader.
Yeah. Mm-hmm. You couldn't read music at all before you went there?
Oh no, I had never taken any listening. I could play a few chords on the guitar, because I'd be around the house with my dad and him, yeah.
Father, huh? I don't think I asked you, how long were you with Perkins?

Well, I'd say about a little over two years I studied with him, yeah. He always wanted me. In fact, he had a lawnmower, he flat peck on, but I never could see how I could blow anything. I never could get my lips strong enough to blow it. I could read the thing and fingers, but I never did like blowing instruments.
Do you still play violin or something?

No, I haven't fooled the violin. When I was playing with the Bay Ridley band on the Pelican, I used it up there a while, because I could only read, I mean, play what I see at that time. I didn't learn how to fake much on it. Oh.
What kind of banjo have you got?

Well, I have a Viga banjo. I was using the Viga banjo then, but when I got on the boat with Fate, well, I was making pretty good money and I bought me a Paramount, and I remember that was a $375 banjo in those days.
Yeah, in those days. It was a pretty good banjo.
It was. The Bay Ridley band, well, they always were a high priced banjo.
That was a tenor?
Oh, yeah, it was a tenor banjo, strictly, yeah.
It was a tenor you use today.
Yeah, that's all I played was tenor banjo.
You never did play G, G banjo, banjo, you know, what are they called?

You got a five string banjo? Yeah. No, that's a little different. I know where they play that. But as far as the Ghetto banjo, I knew I could play that, because I just liked the other, the other guitar.

Yeah. Can you remember any other banjo players, when you got back to New Orleans, you know, when you got back the final time that impressed you? Yeah. About 56, who else was playing around about then?
Around 56.
Well, when you got back into New Orleans.

Yeah, well, I got back in Chicago in 49. Yeah. Oh, yeah, Halston Verrett, he was still playing. George Gino was still playing. Mm-hmm. And, uh, uh, Fred Miner, we call him H.A. Miner, was still playing the banjo. And, uh, see, that's all. There was a terrific guy around here in the 30s, was named Penn. Mm-hmm. He was another terrific picker, but I think he had, he had died somewhere in, uh, in the 40s, I think. Mm-hmm. I think it was our late 40s, like that, or maybe the early 50.
Mm-hmm.
He was with the WPA band, all the musicians, remember. You know, he probably wouldn't have told no more. Yeah, yeah. He was a terrific picker, yeah.
You weren't with the WPA at all, wasn't he?

No, I didn't go because I could always do better without the WPA. I mean, I was working with bands like Sidney and Poulon, and I had other guys I'd be working with when, uh, the big band wouldn't be working, you know? But, like, this time of year, say, from the holiday, Christmas holidays, and to Mardi Gras, man, we'd be busy. Yeah. Only time we'd have a break was after, uh, Mardi Gras, between Mardi Gras and during the Lent, see? Mm-hmm. And those days.
And, uh, you were just, like, gigging around now, you know? I mean, you were just freelancing now?
Well, that's what I'm doing here. I'd plan with bands like that.
